vote.evidence: The first half of the claim is quote-supported: the PRSA blog post (PRsay, 2012-07-20, by then-Chair/CEO Gerard F. Corbett) does state that issuing a news release carries implicit consent to re-use and publish its content, with exceptions (attribution recommended for direct quotes, facts/figures). But the operative second sentence — that this "materially lowers the practical copyright/permission risk of ingesting, storing, and transforming corporate press releases in an aggregation product" — is an overreach the source does not support and case law contradicts. (1) Context mismatch: the PRSA post addressed whether a JOURNALIST'S unattributed use of release text in news coverage is plagiarism (triggered by a 2012 Kansas City Star firing); it says nothing about commercial products that systematically ingest, store, and republish transformed content — an implied license is bounded by the purpose of distribution, and a trade association's blog cannot grant a license only copyright holders can grant. (2) Directly contradicting authority: in MidlevelU/ThriveAP v. ACI Information Group (11th Cir. 2021) the court REJECTED the implied-license defense for an aggregator that scraped freely-published RSS content and republished computer-generated summaries plus full text — almost exactly the proposed product's use pattern; AP v. Meltwater (S.D.N.Y. 2013) likewise rejected fair use for a commercial news aggregator's excerpts. (3) The claim ignores contractual risk unaffected by any PRSA norm: PR Newswire, Business Wire, and GlobeNewswire terms of service prohibit systematic retrieval/redistribution, so ingestion from wire sites carries ToS/breach risk regardless of the issuer's implied consent. (4) Source quality/age: a 14-year-old advocacy blog post from the PR industry's own trade association (with an interest in maximizing release pickup) is far too weak to support a legal-risk conclusion about aggregation products, and it predates both Meltwater (2013) and MidlevelU (2021). The narrow factual statement about PRSA's stance is real; the risk-lowering inference attached to it fails.
